summary: Gives an overview of the L-band Digital Aeronautical Communications System, a terrestrial data link for civil aviation. It describes a cellular broadband design with IPv6 support, aimed at reliable and secure communication between aircraft and ground. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Airplanes need a dependable radio data link to the ground. This explains a new one built to carry internet-style messages safely.

subtitle: A new digital radio system for aircraft to talk safely to air traffic control.

tldr.problem: Aircraft use VHF voice radio (since 1948) and narrowband data links to talk to air traffic control, but these are saturated in busy airspace and cannot handle modern data needs. Aviation needs a secure, high-speed terrestrial data link to support new flight guidance systems.
tldr.mechanism: The L-Band Digital Aeronautical Communications System (LDACS) is a cellular broadband system operating in protected aviation spectrum. It delivers 300 to 1400 kilobits per second, supports IPv6, includes built-in security, and handles priorities to guarantee service for safety-critical messages while also supporting airline business communications.
tldr.outcome: LDACS is standardized by ICAO and EUROCAE and has been tested in flight trials. It is planned as a foundational piece of the Future Communications Infrastructure (FCI), working alongside satellite systems to provide reliable, multihomed global coverage for IPv6-based aeronautical networking.

today: RFC 9372 provides informational context on LDACS at a snapshot in time (May 2022). LDACS standardization by ICAO is not yet complete; technical manuals are planned for completion by end of 2023. The system has been validated in ground and flight trials and is expected to begin rollout starting in Central Europe. IPv6 integration work is ongoing, with ICAO seeking IETF guidance on reliable IP operation over LDACS.

sections.title: The Need for Modern Aeronautical Communications
sections.content:
Aviation is shifting from analog to digital communications and from proprietary systems to IP-based networking. Currently, voice communications use VHF double-sideband amplitude modulation (DSB-AM), a reliable but spectrum-inefficient analog technique in use since 1948. Data communications use narrowband systems with throughput in the kilobit-per-second range, creating bottlenecks for modern applications like trajectory negotiation and real-time weather data.

The LDACS (L-band Digital Aeronautical Communications System) addresses this by providing a terrestrial cellular broadband system operating in spectrum licensed for aviation. It supports both Air Traffic Service (ATS) messages (flight guidance) and Aeronautical Operational Control (AOC) messages (airline business communications), with built-in security and service prioritization. ICAO has standardized LDACS in the Global Air Navigation Plan (GANP) for rollout starting in Central Europe.
sections.plainLanguage: Old radio is slow and uses a lot of spectrum. LDACS is faster, more secure, and digital, like the difference between Morse code and texting.

sections.title: System Architecture and Protocol Stack
sections.content:
LDACS is designed as a multi-application cellular broadband system with seamless handover between cells and decoupled physical and operational coverage. The system operates in the L-band (960–1164 MHz), protected spectrum used only for aviation. Ground-Stations (GSs) provide cellular coverage, and Aircraft Stations (ASs) connect to them.

The protocol stack consists of a Physical Layer based on OFDM (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing) with QPSK modulation, a Data Link Layer providing Medium Access Control and Logical Link Control, and a Subnetwork Layer that handles IPv6 encapsulation. The RFC notes that LDACS defines 1536-byte user data packets for IPv6 traffic, with optional support for Robust Header Compression (ROHC) to reduce overhead. Management interfaces use NETCONF and SNMP protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: LDACS has layers like a sandwich: the bottom is radio signals, the middle is the rules for sharing the radio, and the top carries Internet messages.

sections.title: Capabilities: Speed, Security, and Priorities
sections.content:
LDACS offers forward-link data rates of 315 to 1428 kilobits per second (ground-to-air) and reverse-link rates of 294 to 1390 kilobits per second (air-to-ground), depending on coding and modulation—up to two orders of magnitude faster than the VHF Data Link mode 2 (VDLm2) system. This enables applications previously impossible over narrowband links.

The system includes built-in security mechanisms: Mutual Authentication and Key Establishment (MAKE) protocols, key derivation and management, message confidentiality and integrity protection, secure logging, and robustness measures. Service priorities allow LDACS to guarantee bandwidth and low latency for safety-critical ATS applications (CPDLC, Context Management, ADS-C) while simultaneously accommodating non-critical AOC services.

Beyond communications, LDACS signals can be used for navigation. Flight trials in 2019 demonstrated positioning accuracy of 171 meters in a four-ground-station setup, offering a backup during GNSS outages or jamming.
sections.plainLanguage: LDACS is fast and secure, so planes can send both urgent safety messages and routine business information. It can also help planes figure out where they are.

sections.title: The Future Communications Infrastructure and Multilink Concept
sections.content:
LDACS is one component of the Future Communications Infrastructure (FCI), which combines terrestrial (LDACS) and satellite systems into a multilink architecture. Different links have complementary strengths: LDACS excels in dense air-traffic areas (continental, airports) with good ground coverage, while satellite systems serve remote and oceanic regions. The aircraft will be multihomed over IPv6, automatically switching between available links based on signal quality and coverage.

The FCI uses Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) for local mobility within an LDACS access network and Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) for global mobility between different FCI links. This work is led by ICAO's Communication Panel Working Group and involves cooperation with the IETF. As of 2022, ICAO and European standardization bodies (EUROCAE) are developing technical manuals; implementation is expected by 2023 onwards.
sections.plainLanguage: LDACS is one radio option. Planes will use both ground-based and satellite options together, picking the best signal as they fly across different regions.

sections.title: Reliability, Availability, and Security Posture
sections.content:
Aviation regulations (RTCA DO-350A/EUROCAE ED-228A) define continuity, availability, and integrity requirements at multiple scopes for each ATM application. LDACS is designed to meet these stringent requirements, which vary by application severity: ATS (flight guidance) demands highest availability; AOC (business communications) lower levels.

The RFC notes that LDACS standardization has focused first on the Physical and Data Link Layers; higher layers (including IPv6 integration) are newer work. Current LDACS specifications do not include a formal "IPv6 over LDACS" standard; SESAR2020 is experimenting with IPv6, and ICAO has sought IETF guidance. Security in LDACS is implemented at the link layer with encryption and authentication, creating a secure foundation. Beyond link-layer security, LDACS must integrate with IPv6 operational security, which is an active area of coordination between ICAO and the IETF.
sections.plainLanguage: LDACS must be very reliable because airplane safety depends on it. Security is built into the radio layer, protecting all messages that travel through it.
